simple: several computers that work together over a network and look like one service to the people using it.
analogy: the book-swap club run by three friends in three towns.
precise: a collection of independent computers that communicate only by passing messages over a network and coordinate to provide a service; there is no shared memory and no shared clock between them.
source: D2 of F5-08 (Maarten van Steen, Andrew S. Tanenbaum, "Distributed Systems" (tier 3; edition to be recorded): the introduction (definition, goals, pitfalls of distributed systems) and the fault-tolerance chapter (availability)); D1 of F5-08 (Martin Kleppmann, "Designing Data-Intensive Applications" (tier 3; edition to be recorded): the opening chapter on reliability, scalability and maintainability (faults versus failures, describing load and performance, percentiles), and the chapter on the trouble with distributed systems (partial failure, unreliable networks and clocks)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: one computer (or one running program) that is part of a distributed system.
analogy: one friend with her shelf and her notebook.
precise: a participant in a distributed system with its own processor, memory and local clock, reachable only through messages; in this course a node is usually one process.
source: D2 of F5-08 (Maarten van Steen, Andrew S. Tanenbaum, "Distributed Systems" (tier 3; edition to be recorded): the introduction (definition, goals, pitfalls of distributed systems) and the fault-tolerance chapter (availability)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: how well a system keeps up when it gets more work, if you give it more machines.
analogy: whether adding a friend lets the club answer more letters.
precise: the ability of a system to handle a growing load (requests per second, data volume, users) by adding resources, while meeting its performance goals; it must be stated with a load measure and a goal.
source: D1 of F5-08 (Martin Kleppmann, "Designing Data-Intensive Applications" (tier 3; edition to be recorded): the opening chapter on reliability, scalability and maintainability (faults versus failures, describing load and performance, percentiles), and the chapter on the trouble with distributed systems (partial failure, unreliable networks and clocks)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a fault is something going wrong inside one part; a failure is the whole service not doing its job.
analogy: Amara catching the flu is a fault; the club stopping is a failure.
precise: a fault is a component deviating from its specification; a failure is the system as a whole no longer providing the required service; fault tolerance means preventing faults from becoming failures.
source: D1 of F5-08 (Martin Kleppmann, "Designing Data-Intensive Applications" (tier 3; edition to be recorded): the opening chapter on reliability, scalability and maintainability (faults versus failures, describing load and performance, percentiles), and the chapter on the trouble with distributed systems (partial failure, unreliable networks and clocks)); D2 of F5-08 (Maarten van Steen, Andrew S. Tanenbaum, "Distributed Systems" (tier 3; edition to be recorded): the introduction (definition, goals, pitfalls of distributed systems) and the fault-tolerance chapter (availability)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: some machines are broken while others still work, and the working ones may not know which.
analogy: Chidi still answers letters while Amara is ill, and he is not sure she is ill.
precise: a state in which some components of a distributed system have failed and others have not, often without the working ones being able to tell which have failed; one machine on its own usually either works or crashes as a whole.
source: D1 of F5-08 (Martin Kleppmann, "Designing Data-Intensive Applications" (tier 3; edition to be recorded): the opening chapter on reliability, scalability and maintainability (faults versus failures, describing load and performance, percentiles), and the chapter on the trouble with distributed systems (partial failure, unreliable networks and clocks)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the fraction of time the service works when someone wants to use it.
analogy: the share of days on which the club can lend a book.
precise: the probability that a system is operational at a given moment, or the fraction of a period during which it is; often written as a decimal (0.999) and computed from the availabilities of its parts under stated assumptions.
source: D2 of F5-08 (Maarten van Steen, Andrew S. Tanenbaum, "Distributed Systems" (tier 3; edition to be recorded): the introduction (definition, goals, pitfalls of distributed systems) and the fault-tolerance chapter (availability)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: several parts breaking at the same time for the same reason.
analogy: two friends in the same town both cut off by one snowstorm.
precise: failures of several components that are not independent because they share a cause (a power feed, a network switch, a software release, a building); the probability of simultaneous failure is then much higher than the product of the individual probabilities.
source: D1 of F5-08 (Martin Kleppmann, "Designing Data-Intensive Applications" (tier 3; edition to be recorded): the opening chapter on reliability, scalability and maintainability (faults versus failures, describing load and performance, percentiles), and the chapter on the trouble with distributed systems (partial failure, unreliable networks and clocks)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: one request that has to ask many servers before it can answer.
analogy: Amara can only reply once all the friends she wrote to have written back.
precise: the number of sub-requests a single request sends in parallel (for example to every partition of the data); the request completes when the slowest needed sub-request completes.
source: D1 of F5-08 (Martin Kleppmann, "Designing Data-Intensive Applications" (tier 3; edition to be recorded): the opening chapter on reliability, scalability and maintainability (faults versus failures, describing load and performance, percentiles), and the chapter on the trouble with distributed systems (partial failure, unreliable networks and clocks)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: asking a program on another computer to run a function for you and send back the answer.
analogy: phoning a friend and asking her to do something (registered F5 mapping).
precise: a communication pattern in which a client invokes a named procedure with arguments on a server by sending a request message and waiting for a reply message carrying the result or an error; libraries make it look like a local function call.
source: D2 of F5-09 (Maarten van Steen, Andrew S. Tanenbaum, "Distributed Systems" (tier 3; edition to be recorded): the communication chapter (remote procedure call, stubs, parameter passing, marshalling) and the fault-tolerance chapter (RPC semantics in the presence of failures; at-least-once, at-most-once; idempotent operations)); D1 of F5-09 (Martin Kleppmann, "Designing Data-Intensive Applications" (tier 3; edition to be recorded): the chapter on encoding and evolution (formats for data, schema evolution, dataflow through services and RPC, the problems with RPC) and the chapter on the trouble with distributed systems (timeouts, unbounded delays)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a small function that looks like the real one but actually sends a message.
analogy: the note Bao reads from when he phones, so every call is asked the same way.
precise: the client-side function (client stub) that marshals arguments into a request, sends it and unmarshals the reply; the server-side counterpart (server stub or skeleton) unmarshals the request and calls the implementation. Often generated from an interface description.
source: D2 of F5-09 (Maarten van Steen, Andrew S. Tanenbaum, "Distributed Systems" (tier 3; edition to be recorded): the communication chapter (remote procedure call, stubs, parameter passing, marshalling) and the fault-tolerance chapter (RPC semantics in the presence of failures; at-least-once, at-most-once; idempotent operations)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: turning the function's arguments into bytes that can travel, and back.
analogy: spelling a name letter by letter on the phone so it arrives exactly.
precise: encoding typed values into a defined byte representation (field order, sizes, byte order) for a message, and decoding them on the other side; the RPC form of serialisation (SP201).
source: D2 of F5-09 (Maarten van Steen, Andrew S. Tanenbaum, "Distributed Systems" (tier 3; edition to be recorded): the communication chapter (remote procedure call, stubs, parameter passing, marshalling) and the fault-tolerance chapter (RPC semantics in the presence of failures; at-least-once, at-most-once; idempotent operations)); D1 of F5-09 (Martin Kleppmann, "Designing Data-Intensive Applications" (tier 3; edition to be recorded): the chapter on encoding and evolution (formats for data, schema evolution, dataflow through services and RPC, the problems with RPC) and the chapter on the trouble with distributed systems (timeouts, unbounded delays)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a number on every request so its answer and any repeat can be recognised.
analogy: "this is request number 7 from Bao".
precise: an identifier chosen by the client, unique per client, carried in the request and echoed in the reply; the pair (client id, request id) identifies one logical operation across retries.
source: D2 of F5-09 (Maarten van Steen, Andrew S. Tanenbaum, "Distributed Systems" (tier 3; edition to be recorded): the communication chapter (remote procedure call, stubs, parameter passing, marshalling) and the fault-tolerance chapter (RPC semantics in the presence of failures; at-least-once, at-most-once; idempotent operations)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: an operation that has the same effect whether you do it once or several times.
analogy: "set my count to ten books" (safe to repeat) versus "add ten books" (not safe).
precise: an operation f with f(f(state)) = f(state) for the same arguments; repeating it after an unknown outcome cannot change the result.
source: D2 of F5-09 (Maarten van Steen, Andrew S. Tanenbaum, "Distributed Systems" (tier 3; edition to be recorded): the communication chapter (remote procedure call, stubs, parameter passing, marshalling) and the fault-tolerance chapter (RPC semantics in the presence of failures; at-least-once, at-most-once; idempotent operations)); D1 of F5-09 (Martin Kleppmann, "Designing Data-Intensive Applications" (tier 3; edition to be recorded): the chapter on encoding and evolution (formats for data, schema evolution, dataflow through services and RPC, the problems with RPC) and the chapter on the trouble with distributed systems (timeouts, unbounded delays)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: either "keep asking until you get an answer, even if it happens twice" or "ask once, even if it may not happen".
analogy: phoning back after a dropped line versus never phoning back.
precise: RPC semantics under failure: at-least-once retries until a reply arrives, so the procedure may execute more than once; at-most-once never executes a request twice, either by not retrying or by detecting duplicates at the server; "exactly-once" effects are obtained by at-least-once delivery plus duplicate detection or idempotence.
source: D2 of F5-09 (Maarten van Steen, Andrew S. Tanenbaum, "Distributed Systems" (tier 3; edition to be recorded): the communication chapter (remote procedure call, stubs, parameter passing, marshalling) and the fault-tolerance chapter (RPC semantics in the presence of failures; at-least-once, at-most-once; idempotent operations)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: how long the caller waits for an answer before deciding something went wrong.
analogy: how long Bao listens to silence before hanging up.
precise: a bound after which the client stops waiting for a reply; it tells the client only that no reply arrived in time, not whether the server executed the request.
source: D1 of F5-09 (Martin Kleppmann, "Designing Data-Intensive Applications" (tier 3; edition to be recorded): the chapter on encoding and evolution (formats for data, schema evolution, dataflow through services and RPC, the problems with RPC) and the chapter on the trouble with distributed systems (timeouts, unbounded delays)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open); R2 of F5-09 (university/labs/F5-09/retry.log: Listing 3 with Listing 1, same toolchain, exit code 0)

simple: how far apart the clocks of two computers are at the same moment.
analogy: everyone's watch is a little different (registered F5 mapping).
precise: the difference between the readings of two nodes' clocks at the same instant; not the same as clock skew in digital circuits, where the term means the difference in arrival time of one clock edge at two flip-flops (clock skew, HW201).
source: D2 of F5-10 (Maarten van Steen, Andrew S. Tanenbaum, "Distributed Systems" (tier 3; edition to be recorded): the coordination chapter (clock synchronization, physical clocks, Cristian's method, logical clocks, Lamport's logical clocks, vector clocks)); D1 of F5-10 (Martin Kleppmann, "Designing Data-Intensive Applications" (tier 3; edition to be recorded): the chapter on the trouble with distributed systems (unreliable clocks, time-of-day versus monotonic clocks, process pauses, leases, fencing tokens)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a clock running a little too fast or too slow, so the error grows over time.
analogy: a watch that gains a few seconds every day.
precise: the rate at which a clock's reading departs from a reference time, caused by the oscillator's frequency error; drift turns a small skew into a large one unless the clock is corrected periodically.
source: D2 of F5-10 (Maarten van Steen, Andrew S. Tanenbaum, "Distributed Systems" (tier 3; edition to be recorded): the coordination chapter (clock synchronization, physical clocks, Cristian's method, logical clocks, Lamport's logical clocks, vector clocks)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: event a happened before event b if a could have influenced b.
analogy: Amara posting a letter happened before Bao reading it, and before anything Bao wrote after reading it.
precise: the smallest relation → with: if a and b are on the same node and a comes first, a → b; if a is the sending of a message and b its receipt, a → b; if a → b and b → c, then a → c. It is a partial order.
source: D3 of F5-10 (Leslie Lamport, "Time, Clocks, and the Ordering of Events in a Distributed System", Communications of the ACM, 1978 (tier 5): the happened-before relation, logical clocks and the clock condition, the total ordering and its use for mutual exclusion, anomalous behaviour and physical clocks) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: two events where neither could have influenced the other.
analogy: Chidi writing in his diary while Amara posts a letter to Bao.
precise: events a and b with neither a → b nor b → a (written a ∥ b); "concurrent" here says nothing about the physical times at which they happened.
source: D3 of F5-10 (Leslie Lamport, "Time, Clocks, and the Ordering of Events in a Distributed System", Communications of the ACM, 1978 (tier 5): the happened-before relation, logical clocks and the clock condition, the total ordering and its use for mutual exclusion, anomalous behaviour and physical clocks) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a counter on each node that makes causes always get smaller numbers than their effects.
analogy: numbering every letter and jumping your own counter past any number you receive.
precise: a logical clock L kept by each node: increment before each event; attach L to each message sent; on receipt set L to max(L, received) and then increment. It satisfies the clock condition: a → b implies L(a) < L(b). Ordering by (L, node id) gives a total order consistent with →.
source: D3 of F5-10 (Leslie Lamport, "Time, Clocks, and the Ordering of Events in a Distributed System", Communications of the ACM, 1978 (tier 5): the happened-before relation, logical clocks and the clock condition, the total ordering and its use for mutual exclusion, anomalous behaviour and physical clocks) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a list of counters, one per node, that tells you exactly which events could have influenced which.
analogy: each letter carries a little table: "how many entries from each friend I have heard about".
precise: a vector V with one entry per node; a node increments its own entry before each event, attaches V to messages, and on receipt takes the element-wise maximum before incrementing; then a → b exactly when V(a) ≤ V(b) element-wise and V(a) ≠ V(b).
source: D2 of F5-10 (Maarten van Steen, Andrew S. Tanenbaum, "Distributed Systems" (tier 3; edition to be recorded): the coordination chapter (clock synchronization, physical clocks, Cristian's method, logical clocks, Lamport's logical clocks, vector clocks)); D6 of F5-10 (Giuseppe DeCandia et al., "Dynamo: Amazon's Highly Available Key-value Store" (SOSP 2007; tier 5): use of vector clocks to version data) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: putting every event in one line, with no ties.
analogy: one combined club diary in which every entry has its own place.
precise: an ordering in which any two distinct events are comparable; a total order consistent with → exists (Lamport clocks with a tie-break give one), but it is not unique: concurrent events may be placed either way.
source: D3 of F5-10 (Leslie Lamport, "Time, Clocks, and the Ordering of Events in a Distributed System", Communications of the ACM, 1978 (tier 5): the happened-before relation, logical clocks and the clock condition, the total ordering and its use for mutual exclusion, anomalous behaviour and physical clocks) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a precise list of the ways a part is allowed to go wrong in your design.
analogy: the club agreeing "a friend may fall ill or lose letters, but never lies in a letter".
precise: the assumptions a system's design makes about how components may deviate from their specification (stop, lose messages, be late, behave arbitrarily); a protocol is correct only relative to its failure model.
source: D2 of F5-11 (Maarten van Steen, Andrew S. Tanenbaum, "Distributed Systems" (tier 3; edition to be recorded): the fault-tolerance chapter (failure models: crash, omission, timing, response, arbitrary failures; failure detection; synchronous and asynchronous systems)); D1 of F5-11 (Martin Kleppmann, "Designing Data-Intensive Applications" (tier 3; edition to be recorded): the chapter on the trouble with distributed systems (faults and partial failures, unreliable networks, detecting faults, timeouts and unbounded delays, process pauses, the truth is defined by the majority, fencing tokens, Byzantine faults, system models)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a crashed computer either stays dead, or comes back later having forgotten what was only in its memory.
analogy: a friend who leaves the club for good, or one who returns after an illness with only her written notebook.
precise: crash-stop: a node halts and never takes another step; crash-recovery: a node halts and may restart, losing volatile state but keeping what it wrote to stable storage.
source: D1 of F5-11 (Martin Kleppmann, "Designing Data-Intensive Applications" (tier 3; edition to be recorded): the chapter on the trouble with distributed systems (faults and partial failures, unreliable networks, detecting faults, timeouts and unbounded delays, process pauses, the truth is defined by the majority, fencing tokens, Byzantine faults, system models)); D2 of F5-11 (Maarten van Steen, Andrew S. Tanenbaum, "Distributed Systems" (tier 3; edition to be recorded): the fault-tolerance chapter (failure models: crash, omission, timing, response, arbitrary failures; failure detection; synchronous and asynchronous systems)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a part that sometimes does not send or receive a message, or answers too late.
analogy: letters lost in the post, or arriving after the club meeting.
precise: omission failure: a component fails to send or to receive some messages; timing (performance) failure: a response arrives outside a specified time interval.
source: D2 of F5-11 (Maarten van Steen, Andrew S. Tanenbaum, "Distributed Systems" (tier 3; edition to be recorded): the fault-tolerance chapter (failure models: crash, omission, timing, response, arbitrary failures; failure detection; synchronous and asynchronous systems)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a part that can do anything at all, including sending wrong or contradictory messages.
analogy: a friend who writes different stories to different friends.
precise: an arbitrary failure: a component may produce any output, at any time, including inconsistent messages to different peers, through bugs, corruption or malice; tolerating it needs more replicas and different protocols than crash failures.
source: D2 of F5-11 (Maarten van Steen, Andrew S. Tanenbaum, "Distributed Systems" (tier 3; edition to be recorded): the fault-tolerance chapter (failure models: crash, omission, timing, response, arbitrary failures; failure detection; synchronous and asynchronous systems)); D1 of F5-11 (Martin Kleppmann, "Designing Data-Intensive Applications" (tier 3; edition to be recorded): the chapter on the trouble with distributed systems (faults and partial failures, unreliable networks, detecting faults, timeouts and unbounded delays, process pauses, the truth is defined by the majority, fencing tokens, Byzantine faults, system models)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: what you may assume about how long messages and computations take.
analogy: "letters always arrive within three days" versus "letters arrive eventually, nobody knows when" versus "usually within three days, but sometimes much later".
precise: synchronous: known upper bounds on message delay, processing time and clock drift; asynchronous: no bounds at all; partially synchronous: bounds hold most of the time or after some unknown time, but may be violated for periods.
source: D1 of F5-11 (Martin Kleppmann, "Designing Data-Intensive Applications" (tier 3; edition to be recorded): the chapter on the trouble with distributed systems (faults and partial failures, unreliable networks, detecting faults, timeouts and unbounded delays, process pauses, the truth is defined by the majority, fencing tokens, Byzantine faults, system models)); D2 of F5-11 (Maarten van Steen, Andrew S. Tanenbaum, "Distributed Systems" (tier 3; edition to be recorded): the fault-tolerance chapter (failure models: crash, omission, timing, response, arbitrary failures; failure detection; synchronous and asynchronous systems)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the part of a system that decides which other nodes seem to have failed.
analogy: Chidi deciding Bao is ill because no letter has come.
precise: a module that outputs the set of processes it currently suspects to have crashed, usually from missing heartbeats or replies; characterised by completeness (crashed processes are eventually suspected) and accuracy (correct processes are not suspected, or eventually not).
source: D2 of F5-11 (Maarten van Steen, Andrew S. Tanenbaum, "Distributed Systems" (tier 3; edition to be recorded): the fault-tolerance chapter (failure models: crash, omission, timing, response, arbitrary failures; failure detection; synchronous and asynchronous systems)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a small "I am alive" message sent regularly.
analogy: Bao's Sunday letter.
precise: a periodic message whose only purpose is to show liveness; the receiver suspects the sender when no heartbeat has arrived within a timeout.
source: D2 of F5-11 (Maarten van Steen, Andrew S. Tanenbaum, "Distributed Systems" (tier 3; edition to be recorded): the fault-tolerance chapter (failure models: crash, omission, timing, response, arbitrary failures; failure detection; synchronous and asynchronous systems)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open); R1 of F5-11 (university/labs/F5-11/detector.log: Listing 1, g++ (Ubuntu 13.3.0-6ubuntu2~24.04.1) 13.3.0, Linux x86_64 cloud build container, exit code 0; results of a simulation model)

simple: deciding a computer has died when it is only slow or cut off.
analogy: Chidi taking over Bao's books while Bao's letter is still in the post.
precise: a failure detector suspecting a process that has not crashed; unavoidable in asynchronous and partially synchronous systems, so designs must remain safe when it happens.
source: D1 of F5-11 (Martin Kleppmann, "Designing Data-Intensive Applications" (tier 3; edition to be recorded): the chapter on the trouble with distributed systems (faults and partial failures, unreliable networks, detecting faults, timeouts and unbounded delays, process pauses, the truth is defined by the majority, fencing tokens, Byzantine faults, system models)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open); R1 of F5-11 (university/labs/F5-11/detector.log: Listing 1, g++ (Ubuntu 13.3.0-6ubuntu2~24.04.1) 13.3.0, Linux x86_64 cloud build container, exit code 0; results of a simulation model)

simple: two parts of a system each think they are in charge.
analogy: the phone lines between two towns are down (registered: network partition) and each town elects its own club secretary.
precise: a state in which two nodes or groups both act as the primary or leader, often after a partition or a false suspicion, accepting conflicting updates.
source: D1 of F5-11 (Martin Kleppmann, "Designing Data-Intensive Applications" (tier 3; edition to be recorded): the chapter on the trouble with distributed systems (faults and partial failures, unreliable networks, detecting faults, timeouts and unbounded delays, process pauses, the truth is defined by the majority, fencing tokens, Byzantine faults, system models)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a number that grows every time a new leader is chosen, so that old leaders can be told "no".
analogy: each new club secretary gets a stamp with a higher number, and the library refuses letters stamped with an older number.
precise: a monotonically increasing number (epoch, term) issued with each grant of leadership or a lock and attached to every action; the resource rejects actions carrying a token lower than the highest it has seen.
source: D1 of F5-11 (Martin Kleppmann, "Designing Data-Intensive Applications" (tier 3; edition to be recorded): the chapter on the trouble with distributed systems (faults and partial failures, unreliable networks, detecting faults, timeouts and unbounded delays, process pauses, the truth is defined by the majority, fencing tokens, Byzantine faults, system models)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: keeping copies of the same data on several computers.
analogy: everyone's copy of the shared notebook (registered F5 mapping).
precise: maintaining multiple copies (replicas) of data on different nodes and propagating every change to all of them, so that the data survives node failures and can be read from several places.
source: D1 of F5-12 (Martin Kleppmann, "Designing Data-Intensive Applications" (tier 3; edition to be recorded): the replication chapter (leaders and followers, synchronous versus asynchronous replication, handling node outages and failover, implementation of replication logs, problems with replication lag, multi-leader replication, leaderless replication, handling write conflicts) and the transactions chapter (lost updates)); D2 of F5-12 (Maarten van Steen, Andrew S. Tanenbaum, "Distributed Systems" (tier 3; edition to be recorded): the consistency and replication chapter (reasons for replication, primary-based protocols, replicated-write protocols)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: one of the copies.
analogy: Bao's copy of the notebook.
precise: a node that stores a copy of some data and applies the changes propagated to it.
source: D1 of F5-12 (Martin Kleppmann, "Designing Data-Intensive Applications" (tier 3; edition to be recorded): the replication chapter (leaders and followers, synchronous versus asynchronous replication, handling node outages and failover, implementation of replication logs, problems with replication lag, multi-leader replication, leaderless replication, handling write conflicts) and the transactions chapter (lost updates)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: one computer accepts all changes and copies them to the others.
analogy: the friend who writes the order (registered: leader), posting each change to the others.
precise: single-leader replication: one replica, the primary (leader), executes all writes and sends the resulting changes, in order, to the backups (followers); if the primary fails, a backup is promoted (failover).
source: D1 of F5-12 (Martin Kleppmann, "Designing Data-Intensive Applications" (tier 3; edition to be recorded): the replication chapter (leaders and followers, synchronous versus asynchronous replication, handling node outages and failover, implementation of replication logs, problems with replication lag, multi-leader replication, leaderless replication, handling write conflicts) and the transactions chapter (lost updates)); D2 of F5-12 (Maarten van Steen, Andrew S. Tanenbaum, "Distributed Systems" (tier 3; edition to be recorded): the consistency and replication chapter (reasons for replication, primary-based protocols, replicated-write protocols)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: waiting for the copies before saying "done", or saying "done" first and copying afterwards.
analogy: waiting for Bao's "copied" postcard before telling the member "it's yours", or posting the day's bundle in the evening.
precise: synchronous: the primary acknowledges a write to the client only after the backups (all, or a chosen number) confirm they have it; asynchronous: the primary acknowledges after its local write and propagates later, so acknowledged writes can be lost if it fails.
source: D1 of F5-12 (Martin Kleppmann, "Designing Data-Intensive Applications" (tier 3; edition to be recorded): the replication chapter (leaders and followers, synchronous versus asynchronous replication, handling node outages and failover, implementation of replication logs, problems with replication lag, multi-leader replication, leaderless replication, handling write conflicts) and the transactions chapter (lost updates)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open); R1 of F5-12 (university/labs/F5-12/counter.log: Listing 1, g++ (Ubuntu 13.3.0-6ubuntu2~24.04.1) 13.3.0, Linux x86_64 cloud build container, exit code 0)

simple: how far behind a copy is.
analogy: how many days of loans are still in the post to Chidi.
precise: the delay (in time or in number of changes) between a write being applied at the primary and at a given replica; with asynchronous replication it is unbounded in principle.
source: D1 of F5-12 (Martin Kleppmann, "Designing Data-Intensive Applications" (tier 3; edition to be recorded): the replication chapter (leaders and followers, synchronous versus asynchronous replication, handling node outages and failover, implementation of replication logs, problems with replication lag, multi-leader replication, leaderless replication, handling write conflicts) and the transactions chapter (lost updates)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: switching to a copy when the main computer fails.
analogy: Bao taking over the notebook after the flood.
precise: the procedure of detecting the primary's failure (F5-11), choosing a new primary (preferably the most up-to-date replica), redirecting clients and fencing the old primary.
source: D1 of F5-12 (Martin Kleppmann, "Designing Data-Intensive Applications" (tier 3; edition to be recorded): the replication chapter (leaders and followers, synchronous versus asynchronous replication, handling node outages and failover, implementation of replication logs, problems with replication lag, multi-leader replication, leaderless replication, handling write conflicts) and the transactions chapter (lost updates)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a kind of data that copies can change independently and always merge into the same result.
analogy: each friend counts only her own loans on her own line, and copies of the page are combined by keeping the biggest number on each line.
precise: a conflict-free replicated data type: a data type whose replicas can be updated without coordination and whose merge is commutative, associative and idempotent, so replicas that have seen the same updates converge; a grow-only counter (G-counter) keeps one count per replica, merges by element-wise maximum, and reads the sum.
source: D7 of F5-12 (Marc Shapiro, Nuno Preguiça, Carlos Baquero, Marek Zawirski, "Conflict-free Replicated Data Types" (tier 5; not in the guide's F5 registry, proposed in this course's notes): definition of CRDTs, the G-counter and PN-counter) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open); R1 of F5-12 (university/labs/F5-12/counter.log: Listing 1, g++ (Ubuntu 13.3.0-6ubuntu2~24.04.1) 13.3.0, Linux x86_64 cloud build container, exit code 0)

simple: copies regularly comparing notes and filling in what they are missing.
analogy: friends swapping their notebooks once a month to copy anything they missed.
precise: a background process in which replicas exchange state (or summaries of it) and merge, so that updates lost or missed in transit eventually reach every replica.
source: D6 of F5-12 (Giuseppe DeCandia et al., "Dynamo: Amazon's Highly Available Key-value Store" (SOSP 2007; tier 5): versioning with vector clocks, anti-entropy); D1 of F5-12 (Martin Kleppmann, "Designing Data-Intensive Applications" (tier 3; edition to be recorded): the replication chapter (leaders and followers, synchronous versus asynchronous replication, handling node outages and failover, implementation of replication logs, problems with replication lag, multi-leader replication, leaderless replication, handling write conflicts) and the transactions chapter (lost updates)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the promise a system makes about what reads can return when data has several copies.
analogy: the club's promise about what a member can find in any copy of the notebook (proposed).
precise: a contract between a replicated data store and its clients that specifies which results of read operations are allowed, given the writes performed and their timing and order; the distributed counterpart of a memory consistency model on one machine (memory consistency model).
source: D2 of F5-13 (Maarten van Steen, Andrew S. Tanenbaum, "Distributed Systems" (tier 3; edition to be recorded): the consistency and replication chapter (data-centric consistency models: sequential and causal; client-centric models: monotonic reads, monotonic writes, read-your-writes, writes-follow-reads)); D1 of F5-13 (Martin Kleppmann, "Designing Data-Intensive Applications" (tier 3; edition to be recorded): problems with replication lag (reading your own writes, monotonic reads, consistent prefix reads), leaderless replication and quorums and their limitations, the consistency and consensus chapter (linearizability, its cost, the CAP theorem, ordering guarantees)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the list of reads and writes that clients made, with when each started and finished and what it returned.
analogy: every member's diary of when they looked into or wrote in a notebook, and what they saw.
precise: a record of operation invocations and responses with their real-time intervals and results; consistency models are defined as conditions on histories.
source: D8 of F5-13 (Maurice P. Herlihy, Jeannette M. Wing, "Linearizability: A Correctness Condition for Concurrent Objects" (tier 5; not in the guide's F5 registry, proposed in this course's notes): definition of linearizability on histories) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open); R1 of F5-13 (university/labs/F5-13/histories.log: Listing 1 on histories.in, g++ (Ubuntu 13.3.0-6ubuntu2~24.04.1) 13.3.0, Linux x86_64 cloud build container, exit code 0)

simple: the system behaves as if there were one copy and each operation happened at one instant during its call.
analogy: as if there were only one notebook in the town square, and every reading or writing happened at a single moment while the member was there.
precise: a history is linearizable if there is a total order of its operations that is a legal sequential history of the object and that respects real time: if operation A completed before B was invoked, A precedes B.
source: D8 of F5-13 (Maurice P. Herlihy, Jeannette M. Wing, "Linearizability: A Correctness Condition for Concurrent Objects" (tier 5; not in the guide's F5 registry, proposed in this course's notes): definition of linearizability on histories); D1 of F5-13 (Martin Kleppmann, "Designing Data-Intensive Applications" (tier 3; edition to be recorded): problems with replication lag (reading your own writes, monotonic reads, consistent prefix reads), leaderless replication and quorums and their limitations, the consistency and consensus chapter (linearizability, its cost, the CAP theorem, ordering guarantees)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: if one change could have caused another, everyone sees them in that order; unrelated changes can be seen in different orders.
analogy: nobody can read Bao's answer before Amara's question, but two unrelated news items may arrive in either order.
precise: writes that are related by the happened-before relation (F5-10) are seen by every process in that order; concurrent writes may be seen in different orders by different processes.
source: D2 of F5-13 (Maarten van Steen, Andrew S. Tanenbaum, "Distributed Systems" (tier 3; edition to be recorded): the consistency and replication chapter (data-centric consistency models: sequential and causal; client-centric models: monotonic reads, monotonic writes, read-your-writes, writes-follow-reads)); D1 of F5-13 (Martin Kleppmann, "Designing Data-Intensive Applications" (tier 3; edition to be recorded): problems with replication lag (reading your own writes, monotonic reads, consistent prefix reads), leaderless replication and quorums and their limitations, the consistency and consensus chapter (linearizability, its cost, the CAP theorem, ordering guarantees)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: if people stop changing the data, all copies end up the same, some time later.
analogy: once nobody writes for a while, all the post arrives and the notebooks match.
precise: a liveness guarantee: if no new updates are made to an item, all replicas eventually return the same value; it says nothing about what reads return before then or how long it takes.
source: D1 of F5-13 (Martin Kleppmann, "Designing Data-Intensive Applications" (tier 3; edition to be recorded): problems with replication lag (reading your own writes, monotonic reads, consistent prefix reads), leaderless replication and quorums and their limitations, the consistency and consensus chapter (linearizability, its cost, the CAP theorem, ordering guarantees)); D6 of F5-13 (Giuseppe DeCandia et al., "Dynamo: Amazon's Highly Available Key-value Store" (SOSP 2007; tier 5): N, R, W quorum configuration, sloppy quorums) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: promises to one user: you always see your own changes, and you never see the data go back in time.
analogy: the catalogue Amara opens always has her own entries, and never loses entries she has already seen, whichever town she is in.
precise: client-centric consistency guarantees: read-your-writes requires every read by a client to reflect all of that client's earlier writes; monotonic reads requires that once a client has read a version, its later reads never return an older one.
source: D2 of F5-13 (Maarten van Steen, Andrew S. Tanenbaum, "Distributed Systems" (tier 3; edition to be recorded): the consistency and replication chapter (data-centric consistency models: sequential and causal; client-centric models: monotonic reads, monotonic writes, read-your-writes, writes-follow-reads)); D1 of F5-13 (Martin Kleppmann, "Designing Data-Intensive Applications" (tier 3; edition to be recorded): problems with replication lag (reading your own writes, monotonic reads, consistent prefix reads), leaderless replication and quorums and their limitations, the consistency and consensus chapter (linearizability, its cost, the CAP theorem, ordering guarantees)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: asking enough copies that a read group and a write group must share at least one copy.
analogy: Amara writes in at least two of the three notebooks, and readers look in at least two: one of the two they look in must have her entry.
precise: with N replicas, a write is acknowledged after W replicas store it and a read queries R replicas and takes the highest version; if R + W > N every read set intersects every write set.
source: D6 of F5-13 (Giuseppe DeCandia et al., "Dynamo: Amazon's Highly Available Key-value Store" (SOSP 2007; tier 5): N, R, W quorum configuration, sloppy quorums); D1 of F5-13 (Martin Kleppmann, "Designing Data-Intensive Applications" (tier 3; edition to be recorded): problems with replication lag (reading your own writes, monotonic reads, consistent prefix reads), leaderless replication and quorums and their limitations, the consistency and consensus chapter (linearizability, its cost, the CAP theorem, ordering guarantees)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open); R2 of F5-13 (university/labs/F5-13/quorum.log: Listing 2, same toolchain, exit code 0)

simple: reading an old value after a newer one has been written.
analogy: looking in Chidi's notebook before Amara's letter has arrived.
precise: a read that returns a value older than the latest write that completed before the read began; forbidden by linearizability, allowed by weaker models.
source: D1 of F5-13 (Martin Kleppmann, "Designing Data-Intensive Applications" (tier 3; edition to be recorded): problems with replication lag (reading your own writes, monotonic reads, consistent prefix reads), leaderless replication and quorums and their limitations, the consistency and consensus chapter (linearizability, its cost, the CAP theorem, ordering guarantees)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: splitting a big dataset into parts that live on different machines.
analogy: each town keeps the part of the catalogue for its own range of letters (proposed).
precise: dividing a dataset so that each record belongs to exactly one partition (shard), and placing partitions on different nodes, so that storage and load are spread; usually combined with replication of each partition.
source: D1 of F5-14 (Martin Kleppmann, "Designing Data-Intensive Applications" (tier 3; edition to be recorded): the partitioning chapter (partitioning of key-value data by key range and by hash of key, skewed workloads and relieving hot spots, partitioning and secondary indexes, rebalancing partitions, request routing)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: one of the parts.
analogy: Bao's letters I–P.
precise: a subset of the dataset, defined by a range of keys or a set of hash values, stored and served as a unit and moved as a unit during rebalancing.
source: D1 of F5-14 (Martin Kleppmann, "Designing Data-Intensive Applications" (tier 3; edition to be recorded): the partitioning chapter (partitioning of key-value data by key range and by hash of key, skewed workloads and relieving hot spots, partitioning and secondary indexes, rebalancing partitions, request routing)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: each part holds keys between two boundaries, like the volumes of an encyclopaedia.
analogy: A–H, I–P, Q–Z.
precise: assigning each partition a contiguous range of sorted keys; range queries touch few partitions, but keys that arrive in order (timestamps, counters) all go to the last partition.
source: D1 of F5-14 (Martin Kleppmann, "Designing Data-Intensive Applications" (tier 3; edition to be recorded): the partitioning chapter (partitioning of key-value data by key range and by hash of key, skewed workloads and relieving hot spots, partitioning and secondary indexes, rebalancing partitions, request routing)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open); R1 of F5-14 (university/labs/F5-14/sharding.log: Listing 1, g++ (Ubuntu 13.3.0-6ubuntu2~24.04.1) 13.3.0, Linux x86_64 cloud build container, exit code 0)

simple: each key goes to the part chosen by a hash of the key, which scatters keys evenly.
analogy: each title is turned into a number by a fixed recipe, and the number decides the town.
precise: assigning a key to a partition by a function of hash(key), for example hash(key) mod N or a position on a hash ring; spreads keys evenly but destroys key order, so range queries must ask every partition.
source: D1 of F5-14 (Martin Kleppmann, "Designing Data-Intensive Applications" (tier 3; edition to be recorded): the partitioning chapter (partitioning of key-value data by key range and by hash of key, skewed workloads and relieving hot spots, partitioning and secondary indexes, rebalancing partitions, request routing)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open); R1 of F5-14 (university/labs/F5-14/sharding.log: Listing 1, g++ (Ubuntu 13.3.0-6ubuntu2~24.04.1) 13.3.0, Linux x86_64 cloud build container, exit code 0)

simple: a way of hashing keys to machines so that adding a machine moves only the keys it takes over.
analogy: towns sit at points around a circle of numbers; each book goes to the next town clockwise from its own number; a new town takes books only from its clockwise neighbour.
precise: keys and nodes are hashed onto the same circular space; a key is owned by the first node point at or after its hash; adding or removing a node moves only the keys in the affected arcs, about 1/N of them.
source: D6 of F5-14 (Giuseppe DeCandia et al., "Dynamo: Amazon's Highly Available Key-value Store" (SOSP 2007; tier 5): partitioning with consistent hashing and virtual nodes, preference lists); D1 of F5-14 (Martin Kleppmann, "Designing Data-Intensive Applications" (tier 3; edition to be recorded): the partitioning chapter (partitioning of key-value data by key range and by hash of key, skewed workloads and relieving hot spots, partitioning and secondary indexes, rebalancing partitions, request routing)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open); R1 of F5-14 (university/labs/F5-14/sharding.log: Listing 1, g++ (Ubuntu 13.3.0-6ubuntu2~24.04.1) 13.3.0, Linux x86_64 cloud build container, exit code 0)

simple: letting each machine sit at many places on the circle, so that the shares even out.
analogy: each town gets a hundred small arcs around the circle instead of one big one.
precise: one of V positions on the hash ring assigned to the same physical node; more virtual nodes reduce the variance of each node's share and spread a joining or leaving node's load over many others.
source: D6 of F5-14 (Giuseppe DeCandia et al., "Dynamo: Amazon's Highly Available Key-value Store" (SOSP 2007; tier 5): partitioning with consistent hashing and virtual nodes, preference lists) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open); R1 of F5-14 (university/labs/F5-14/sharding.log: Listing 1, g++ (Ubuntu 13.3.0-6ubuntu2~24.04.1) 13.3.0, Linux x86_64 cloud build container, exit code 0)

simple: moving parts between machines when machines are added, removed or overloaded.
analogy: re-copying catalogue pages to Dara's town when she joins.
precise: changing the assignment of keys or partitions to nodes while the system keeps serving requests, moving as little data as possible and keeping load balanced afterwards.
source: D1 of F5-14 (Martin Kleppmann, "Designing Data-Intensive Applications" (tier 3; edition to be recorded): the partitioning chapter (partitioning of key-value data by key range and by hash of key, skewed workloads and relieving hot spots, partitioning and secondary indexes, rebalancing partitions, request routing)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: one key or part that gets far more requests than the rest.
analogy: everyone asking about "Pebble and the Sea".
precise: a partition whose load is disproportionately high because of skew in the workload, often a single popular key; partitioning by key cannot spread the load of one key, since every request for it goes to the same partition.
source: D1 of F5-14 (Martin Kleppmann, "Designing Data-Intensive Applications" (tier 3; edition to be recorded): the partitioning chapter (partitioning of key-value data by key range and by hash of key, skewed workloads and relieving hot spots, partitioning and secondary indexes, rebalancing partitions, request routing)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open); R2 of F5-14 (university/labs/F5-14/hotshard.log: forensic evidence generator, same toolchain, exit code 0)

simple: finding which machine holds the key you want.
analogy: knowing which town to write to for a given title.
precise: the mechanism that sends a request to the node owning its key: any node forwards, a routing tier forwards, or clients know the partition map; all need an up-to-date map, often kept in a coordination service.
source: D1 of F5-14 (Martin Kleppmann, "Designing Data-Intensive Applications" (tier 3; edition to be recorded): the partitioning chapter (partitioning of key-value data by key range and by hash of key, skewed workloads and relieving hot spots, partitioning and secondary indexes, rebalancing partitions, request routing)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)
